source.title: Generative Medical Event Models Improve with Scale
source.authors: Shane Waxler; Paul J. Blazek; D. White; Daniel Sneider; Kevin Chung; Mani Nagarathnam; P. Williams; H. Voeller; Karen K. Wong; Matthew Swanhorst; Sheng Zhang; N. Usuyama; C. Wong; Tristan Naumann; H. Poon; Andrew J. Loza; Daniella Meeker; Seth Hain; Rahul Shah

record.tranche_reason: The paper applies an isoFLOP scaling-law methodology to a new model and data setting, structured medical-event sequences, and reports fitted compute-optimal scaling relationships.
record.gate_note: The scaling sweep and downstream evaluations report results relevant to scaling and loss-to-performance relationships. The paper also reports many downstream task scores, but those task comparisons do not independently measure the claim’s scaling laws.
record.test_reason: The study runs a Hoffmann-style isoFLOP sweep (10 sizes, 2M–1B parameters, four budgets from 1e18 to 1e19 FLOPs) on structured medical-event sequences rather than natural language. It fits power laws for optimal N and D against compute and relates training loss to downstream clinical scores. This is the original method applied in a new modality, so T3 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also claim the largest medical-event scaling study to date and a 1,000:1 optimal token-to-parameter ratio, unlike NL work. They say downstream performance improves with model scale, with Curiosity-L matching or beating supervised baselines on most tasks. They present training loss as a useful proxy for downstream capability.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the Hoffmann et al. isoFLOP methodology and power-law fitting for compute-optimal parameter and token counts, adapted to structured medical events and Cosmos data rather than natural-language corpora.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream performance rises with the number of simulated timelines n at inference, plateauing around n≳64.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time sampling compute improves downstream performance in generative event models, independently of training compute.

record.problems: The scaling analysis uses four fixed compute budgets and a single structured medical-event dataset, with models ranging from 2 million to 1 billion parameters. No uncertainty estimates for the fitted exponents are reported. The loss-decrease result is stated, but power-law loss fits and small-run-to-large-run loss prediction are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: Many individual downstream task scores and plotted checkpoint results are not separately included because they measure task performance rather than the scaling-law versions, or are available only as plots without numerical values. Scaling-law outcomes are retained as aggregate fits reported by the authors in Section 2.6 and Figure 15.

untested.parts: No natural-language model is trained, and no power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute is reported.
The fitted laws are used to size Curiosity-L (about 1.4e22 FLOPs, roughly 1,000× beyond the sweep). The predicted versus achieved loss of that run is not reported.
Shape is not varied at a fixed parameter count.
The power-law form of the loss itself is not shown. Images, video, repeated data and fine-tuning are not tested.
Fitting method, parameter counting, schedule and curvature away from a power law are not varied or examined.

missing.what: Per-size (S/M/L) downstream scores. Most improve monotonically, but there are exceptions: incident heart attack AUCROC 0.802/0.804/0.801; HbA1c<9 M 0.760 > L 0.756; systemic sclerosis S 0.636 > M 0.618; HLD stroke 1yr S 0.796 > M 0.788.
Minimum loss values per isoFLOP budget, readable only from the plot

record.verdict_notes: The sweep covers only one decade of compute, with four points and no confidence intervals on the exponents. The downstream relationship uses training loss, and the sigmoid fit's prediction of Curiosity-L is not quantified. The paper is by Epic/Microsoft authors and is a preprint. V1 does not apply because the model is trained on medical events rather than language.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports that validation loss decreases predictably with scale, but does not fit or report power-law loss exponents against parameters, tokens, or compute.
It uses fitted compute-optimal allocation curves to set training parameters, but does not test whether loss predictions fitted on small runs accurately predict much larger runs.
The fitted trends are based on four fixed compute budgets and are reported for this medical-event model and dataset; the paper does not establish the trend across other datasets or setups.
Architecture details are not varied at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
The tested setting is structured medical-event pretraining. Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, and transfer regimes are not tested.
The reported downstream relationship covers the paper’s clinical evaluations, not general language-model downstream tasks.

The paper compares its fitted exponents with reported natural-language results and notes a different optimal token-to-parameter ratio, but does not vary fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules, or data within its own experiments, nor test whether curves bend away from power laws.

rows.subject: Curiosity scaling sweep (10 model sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and training tokens in scaling experiments on Cosmos medical-event data.

conditions.value: four fixed compute budgets for isoFLOP experiments

rows.measure: Validation loss as model size and training-token count increase
rows.value: The authors report that increasing parameters and training tokens predictably decreases model loss.
rows.note: This supports a decreasing loss trend in the tested domain, but the paper fits power laws to compute-optimal parameter and token counts, not to loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
rows.check: This is not a natural-language model, so the row does not bear on V1. The paper only says scaling 'predictably decreases' loss. It fits no power law to loss against N, D or C; Figure 15 shows isoFLOP minima with parabola fits only. The row cannot show whether the power-law loss form holds.

rows.subject: Curiosity scaling sweep (10 model sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to compute-optimal parameter count across isoFLOP experiments.
rows.measure: Exponent α for optimal parameter count Nopt as a function of compute C
rows.note: Aggregate fitted result from the scaling sweep.
rows.check: The fit spans only one decade of compute (four budgets, 1e18–1e19 FLOPs). No uncertainty is reported.

rows.subject: Curiosity scaling sweep (10 model sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to compute-optimal training-token count across isoFLOP experiments.
rows.measure: Exponent β for optimal training-token count Dopt as a function of compute C
rows.note: The authors interpret the near-equal exponents as indicating proportional growth of optimal model size and token count with compute.
rows.check: Same narrow compute range as R2 and no uncertainty. The near-equal α and β support Hoffmann-style equal growth.

rows.subject: Curiosity compute-optimal models
rows.operation_detail: Derived the optimal token-to-parameter ratio from the compute-optimal scaling analysis.

conditions.value: Natural-language scaling work discussed by the authors

rows.note: The authors state that this ratio contrasts with natural-language work; they also say their fitted exponents are similar to those reported for natural-language corpora. The natural-language comparison is contextualized through prior work.
rows.check: The natural-language comparison ratio is not given numerically; the contrast with NL work is a cited result. The ratio does show that the compute-optimal split depends on the data domain, while the exponents match the NL values. Implied ratios in Table 1 are about 1,350–1,700:1. Removed the V3 and V5 links.

rows.measure: Downstream performance as a function of training loss
rows.value: The authors report a smooth, sigmoidal relationship between training loss and downstream scores across different model sizes and compute budgets.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result reported across the named task groups; the fitted curve excluded Curiosity-L.
rows.check: Downstream scores are plotted against training loss, not held-out loss. The sigmoid was fitted without Curiosity-L 'to assess predictive utility', but how well it predicted Curiosity-L is never quantified.

relationships.condition: Medical-event decoder transformers on Cosmos, compute 1e18–1e19 FLOPs
relationships.reason: α=0.520 and β=0.512 are near-equal, matching Hoffmann's equal growth of model size and data (R2, R3). The compute range spans only one decade.
relationships.display_finding: Optimal model-size and data exponents were 0.520 and 0.512, respectively, over the tested compute decade.
